title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 5–7 (Night 221, continuing nights-220), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 221 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. In the wilderness the old treasurer weeps with al-Amjad and al-Asʿad; the brothers embrace, lay the blame on the scheming of their two mothers, and each recites verses of prayer. Each begs to die first, and they ask to be bound together so that one stroke kills both; the treasurer binds them, draws his sword and asks their last wishes, and al-Amjad charges him to tell the king that he has killed his sons without making sure of their guilt, and to recite to him two verses on the wiles of women; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-first night,
sentences.n: al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-ʿishrūna, “the first and the twenty”: in an ordinal above twenty the unit comes first and is joined to the tens by wa-, and both parts take the case of the noun they describe, here the nominative of al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْخَازِنْدَارَ بَكَى لِبُكَائِهِمَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-khāzindāra bakā li-bukāʾihimā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-treasurer wept at-their-weeping.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the treasurer wept to see the two brothers weep.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the last words of the night before. li-bukāʾihimā: li- of cause, “at their weeping”; -himā, “their”, is dual: al-Amjad and al-Asʿad. The ئ of لبكائهما is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْأَخَوَيْنِ تَعَانَقَا وَوَدَّعَا بَعْضَهُمَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-akhawayni taʿānaqā wa-waddaʿā baʿḍahumā
sentences.l: Then (indeed) the-two-brothers embraced-one-another and-bade-farewell-to each-other.
sentences.i: Then the two brothers embraced and bade each other farewell.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, only moves the story on. taʿānaqā, Form VI of ʿ-n-q (ʿunuq, “neck”), “to embrace one another”: Form VI is the form of doing something mutually, and the dual ending -ā shows that two do it. baʿḍahumā, literally “some of the two of them”, is the later idiom for “each other”, where Classical would say baʿḍuhumā baʿḍan. The shadda of وودّعا is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ أَحَدُهُمَا لِلْآخَرِ إِنَّ هٰذِهِ كُلَّهُ مِنْ كَيْدِ الْخَائِنَتَيْنِ أُمِّي وَأُمِّكَ وَهٰذَا جَزَاءُ مَاجَرَى مِنِّي فِي حَقِّ أُمِّكَ وَجَزَاءُ مَاجَرَى مِنْكَ فِي حَقِّ أُمِّي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla aḥaduhumā li-al-ākhari inna hādhihi kullahu min kaydi al-khāʾinatayni ummī wa-ummika wa-hādhā jazāʾu mā jarā minnī fī ḥaqqi ummika wa-jazāʾu mā jarā minka fī ḥaqqi ummī
sentences.l: And-said one-of-them-two to-the-other: Indeed this, all-of-it, (is) from (the) scheming (of) the-two-treacherous-women, my-mother and-your-mother; and-this (is the) recompense (of) what-passed from-me in (the) regard (of) your-mother, and-(the)-recompense (of) what-passed from-you in (the) regard (of) my-mother.
sentences.i: And one of them said to the other: All this comes of the scheming of those two treacherous women, my mother and yours; and this is our requital for what passed between me and your mother, and between you and mine.
sentences.n: inna hādhihi kullahu, “indeed this, all of it”: the print joins the feminine demonstrative hādhihi to a masculine kullahu; the agreement is loose, as often in this Arabic, and is vocalised as printed. kullahu follows the noun of inna as an emphasis and shares its accusative. al-khāʾinatayni, “the two treacherous women”: feminine dual of khāʾin, active participle of khāna, “to betray”, genitive after kayd; ummī wa-ummika stand in apposition to it. jazāʾu mā jarā minnī fī ḥaqqi ummika, “the recompense of what passed from me with regard to your mother”: each brother has refused the advances of the other's mother, and each mother has accused her stepson to the king. fī ḥaqqi, “with regard to, toward”. The print runs mā jarā together as ماجرى, as it often does; it is kept as set. The آ of للآخر, the ئ of الخائنتين, the ء of جزاء and the shaddas of كلّه, امّي, امّك and منّي are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللّٰهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ إِنَّا لِلّٰهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi innā li-llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūna
sentences.l: So-(there-is)-no power and-no-strength except in-God, the-High, the-Mighty. Indeed-we (are) to-God, and-indeed-we to-Him (are) returning.
sentences.i: There is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Almighty. We belong to God, and to Him we return.
sentences.n: Two stock formulas of resignation. lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata: the lā of absolute negation takes its noun in the accusative without tanwīn, “there is no power”; the print runs wa-lā quwwata together as ولاقوة. illā bi-Allāhi: bi-, “in, through”, marks the one from whom all power comes. innā li-llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūna is Qurʾān 2:156, said in the face of death or disaster: li- of belonging, “we are God's”. The shaddas of انّا and وانّا are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْأَسْعَدَ اعْتَنَقَ أَخَاهُ وَصَعَّدَ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-Asʿada iʿtanaqa akhāhu wa-ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then (indeed) al-Asʿad embraced his-brother and-sent-up the-sighs and-recited these verses:
sentences.i: Then al-Asʿad embraced his brother, heaved deep sighs and recited these verses:
sentences.n: iʿtanaqa, Form VIII of ʿ-n-q, “to embrace”, done by one to another, where Form VI taʿānaqa was mutual. ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti, “he sent up the sighs”: Form II of ṣ-ʿ-d, “to make rise”. hādhihi al-abyāta: a non-human plural takes the feminine singular demonstrative.

sentences.t:
يَا مَنْ اِلَيْهِ الْمُشْتَكَى وَالْمَفْزَعُ * اَنْتَ الْمُعَدُّ لِكُلِّ مَا يُتَوَقَّعُ
مَالِيْ سِوَى قَرْعِي لِبَابِكَ حِيْلَةٌ * وَلَئِنْ رُدِدْتُ فَاَيُّ بَابٍ اَقْرَعُ
يَا مَنْ خَزَائِنُ فَضْلِهِ فِي قَوْلِ كُنْ * اُمْنُنْ فَاِنَّ الْخَيْرَ عِنْدَكَ اَجْمَعُ
sentences.tr:
yā man ilayhi al-mushtakā wa-al-mafzaʿu * anta al-muʿaddu li-kulli mā yutawaqqaʿu
mā lī siwā qarʿī li-bābika ḥīlatun * wa-laʾin rudidtu fa-ayyu bābin aqraʿu
yā man khazāʾinu faḍlihi fī qawli kun * umnun fa-inna al-khayra ʿindaka ajmaʿu
sentences.l:
O one to-whom (is) the-complaint and-the-refuge, * You (are) the-one-held-ready for-every-thing that is-awaited.
Not to-me, besides my-knocking at-your-door, (is) a-means; * and-if I-am-turned-back, then-which door shall-I-knock?
O one-whose treasuries (of) his-bounty (are) in (the) saying (of) “Be!”, * be-gracious, for indeed the-good with-you (is) all-together.
sentences.i:
O You to whom all complaint is brought, in whom is all refuge, * You are the One held ready for all that may befall.
I have no recourse but to knock at Your door; * and if I am turned away, at what door shall I knock?
O You whose treasuries of bounty lie in the word “Be!”, * be gracious, for all good is with You.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and the lines rhyme in -aʿu: al-mafzaʿu, yutawaqqaʿu, aqraʿu, ajmaʿu; the first line rhymes within itself. The prayer is addressed to God. al-mushtakā, “the one to whom complaint is made”, and al-mafzaʿ, “the place of refuge”, are nouns of place, from Form VIII ishtakā and Form I faziʿa. al-muʿadd, “the one held ready”, passive participle of Form IV aʿadda; mā yutawaqqaʿu, “what is expected”, Form V passive. mā lī … ḥīlatun, “I have no means”: mā negates and li- marks the one who has; the print sets mā lī as one word, مَالِيْ, and puts a sukūn on the long vowels of مَالِيْ and حِيْلَةٌ. qarʿī li-bābika, “my knocking at your door”: li- here marks what is knocked on. wa-laʾin, “and if indeed”: la- adds the force of an oath to in, “if”. rudidtu, “I am turned back”, passive of radda: before a consonant ending the doubled root is written out, r-d-d. fī qawli kun, “in the saying of ‘Be!’”: God's creative command, kun fa-yakūnu, “Be! and it is”, in the Qurʾān. umnun, “be gracious, bestow”, imperative of manna, with its two nūns unmerged, اُمْنُنْ. ajmaʿu, “all together, entire”. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare: اِلَيْهِ, اَنْتَ, فَاَيُّ, اَقْرَعُ, اُمْنُنْ, فَاِنَّ, اَجْمَعُ.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْأَمْجَدُ بُكَاءَ أَخِيهِ بَكَى وَضَمَّهُ إِلَى صَدْرِهِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-Amjadu bukāʾa akhīhi bakā wa-ḍammahu ilā ṣadrihi wa-anshada hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And-when heard al-Amjad (the) weeping (of) his-brother, he-wept, and-pressed-him to his-breast, and-recited these-two verses:
sentences.i: When al-Amjad heard his brother weeping, he wept too, clasped him to his breast and recited these two verses:
sentences.n: The print has صدرة, a misprint for صدره, corrected here. ḍammahu ilā ṣadrihi, “he pressed him to his breast”: ḍamma takes ilā for what one draws a person against. The ء of بكاء and the shadda of وضمّه are printed.

sentences.t:
يَا مَنْ اَيَادِيهِ عِنْدِي غَيْرُ وَاحِدَةٍ * وَمَنْ مَوَاهِبُهُ تَنْمُو عَنِ الْعَدَدِ
مَا نَابَنِي مِنْ زَمَانِي قَطُّ نَائِبَةٌ * اِلَّا وَجَدْتُكَ فِيهَا آخِذًا بِيَدِي
sentences.tr:
yā man ayādīhi ʿindī ghayru wāḥidatin * wa-man mawāhibuhu tanmū ʿani al-ʿadadi
mā nābanī min zamānī qaṭṭu nāʾibatun * illā wajadtuka fīhā ākhidhan bi-yadī
sentences.l:
O one-whose favours with-me (are) other-than one, * and-whose gifts grow beyond the-counting,
not befell-me from my-time ever a-misfortune * except I-found-you in-it taking by-my-hand.
sentences.i:
O You whose favours to me are more than one, * whose gifts grow past all counting:
never has a blow of fortune fallen on me * but I found You there in it, holding me by the hand.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -adi / -adī: al-ʿadadi, bi-yadī. These too are addressed to God. ayādī, “favours, benefits”, a plural of yad, “hand”, in the sense of a helping hand; ghayru wāḥidatin, “not (just) one”, means “many”. tanmū ʿani al-ʿadadi, “grow beyond counting”: ʿan of going past. mā nābanī … nāʾibatun illā wajadtuka, “no misfortune befell me but I found you”: mā … illā frames the whole, every misfortune and every rescue. nāba and nāʾiba are verb and noun of one root, n-w-b, a figure the poets like. ākhidhan bi-yadī, “taking hold of my hand”: akhadha takes bi- for what is grasped; ākhidhan is a ḥāl, the state in which he was found.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ لِلْخَازِنْدَارِ سَأَلْتُكَ بِالْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ الْمَلِكِ السَّتَّارِ أَنْ تَقْتُلَنِي قَبْلَ أَخِى الْأَسْعَدِ لَعَلَّ نَارَ قَلْبِي تَخْمُدُ وَلَاتَدَعْهُمَا تَتَوَقَّدُ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla al-Amjadu li-al-khāzindāri saʾaltuka bi-al-wāḥidi al-qahhāri al-maliki al-sattāri an taqtulanī qabla akhī al-Asʿadi laʿalla nāra qalbī takhmudu wa-lā tadaʿhumā tatawaqqadu
sentences.l: Then said al-Amjad to-the-treasurer: I-ask-you by-the-One, the-All-Conquering, the-King, the-Veiler, that you-kill-me before my-brother al-Asʿad; perhaps (the) fire (of) my-heart will-die-down, and-(do)-not leave-them-two blazing.
sentences.i: Then al-Amjad said to the treasurer: I beg you by the One, the All-Conquering, the King who veils our faults, to kill me before my brother al-Asʿad, so that perhaps the fire in my heart may die down; do not leave the two of them to blaze.
sentences.n: saʾaltuka bi-, “I have asked you by”: the perfect of an entreaty made in the speaking, “I beg you by”; bi- marks what one adjures by. al-Wāḥid, al-Qahhār and al-Malik are among the Names of God; al-Sattār, “the One who veils (sins)”, the intensive pattern faʿʿāl of satara, “to cover”, is a common epithet. The names rhyme in pairs, al-qahhār / al-sattār, and the clause ends on a second chime, takhmudu / tatawaqqadu. akhī, “my brother”: the print writes the suffix -ī with ى, اخى. laʿalla takes its noun in the accusative, nāra, with an imperfect as its predicate. wa-lā tadaʿhumā tatawaqqadu, “and do not leave them two blazing”: lā with the jussive tadaʿ (from wadaʿa, “to leave”) forbids, and the imperfect tatawaqqadu, Form V of w-q-d, describes the state left. The dual -humā has no clear antecedent (perhaps the fire and the heart, or the hearts of both brothers), and one would expect tadaʿhā, “leave it”, the fire; the print is kept as it stands, and the sense is plain: do not let the burning go on. The print runs wa-lā tadaʿhumā together as ولاتدعهما. The ء of سألتك and the shaddas of القهّار, الستّار and لعلّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَبَكَي الْأَسْعَدُ وَقَالَ مَا يُقْتَلُ قَبْلُ إِلَّا أَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-bakā al-Asʿadu wa-qāla mā yuqtalu qablu illā anā
sentences.l: And-wept al-Asʿad and-said: Not is-killed first except I.
sentences.i: Al-Asʿad wept and said: No one shall be killed first but me.
sentences.n: The print writes bakā with a dotted ي, فبكي, where the usual spelling has ى; it is read fa-bakā. mā yuqtalu qablu illā anā, “none is killed first but I”: mā … illā restricts, and anā, after illā, is the real subject of the passive yuqtalu. qablu, “before, first”, is the adverb cut off from the noun it would govern, with an invariable -u.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ الرَّأْيُ أَنْ تَعْتَنِقَنِي وَأَعْتَنِقَكَ حَتَّى يَنْزِلَ السَّيْفُ عَلَيْنَا فَيَقْتُلَنَا دَفْعَةً وَاحِدَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu al-raʾyu an taʿtaniqanī wa-aʿtaniqaka ḥattā yanzila al-sayfu ʿalaynā fa-yaqtulanā dafʿatan wāḥidatan
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad: The-counsel (is) that you-embrace-me and-I-embrace-you, until comes-down the-sword upon-us and-kills-us (at) one push.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said: The best course is for you to embrace me and I you, so that the sword comes down on us and kills us both at one stroke.
sentences.n: al-raʾyu an …, “the counsel is that …”: an with the subjunctive makes a clause that stands as the predicate. taʿtaniqanī wa-aʿtaniqaka: the same Form VIII verb, once for each brother. ḥattā yanzila, “until (and so that) it comes down”: ḥattā with the subjunctive, of something still to come, and fa-yaqtulanā continues in the same mood. dafʿatan wāḥidatan, “one push”, that is “at one go”: an adverbial accusative. The ء of الرأي is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اعْتَنَقَ الِاثْنَانِ وَجْهًا لِوَجْهٍ وَالْتَزَمَا بِبَعْضِهِمَا شَدَّهُمَا الْخَازِنْدَارُ وَرَبَطَهُمَا بِالْحِبَالِ وَهُوَ يَبْكِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā iʿtanaqa al-ithnāni wajhan li-wajhin wa-iltazamā bi-baʿḍihimā shaddahumā al-khāzindāru wa-rabaṭahumā bi-al-ḥibāli wa-huwa yabkī
sentences.l: And-when embraced the-two face to-face and-clung to-each-other, bound-them-two the-treasurer and-tied-them-two with-the-ropes, and-he (was) weeping.
sentences.i: So when the two had embraced face to face and held fast to one another, the treasurer bound them and tied them together with ropes, weeping as he did it.
sentences.n: iʿtanaqa al-ithnāni: a verb standing before its subject stays singular even when the subject is dual, as in Classical; once the subject is named, the next verb, iltazamā, is dual. wajhan li-wajhin, “face to face”: li- here “to, against”. iltazama bi-, Form VIII of l-z-m, “to cling to”: bi- marks what one holds fast; bi-baʿḍihimā, “to each other”. shadda, “to bind tight”, and rabaṭa, “to tie”; bi-al-ḥibāli, bi- of the instrument, “with the ropes”. wa-huwa yabkī, “and he weeping”: a circumstantial clause. The shadda of شدّهما is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَرَّدَ سَيْفَهُ وَقَالَ وَاللّٰهِ يَا سَيِّدَايَ إِنَّهُ يَعِزُّ عَلَيَّ قَتْلُكُمَا
sentences.tr: thumma jarrada sayfahu wa-qāla wa-Allāhi yā sayyidāya innahu yaʿizzu ʿalayya qatlukumā
sentences.l: Then he-bared his-sword and-said: By-God, O my-two-masters, indeed-it is-grievous upon-me (the) killing (of) you-two.
sentences.i: Then he drew his sword and said: By God, my masters, it is hard for me to kill you.
sentences.n: yā sayyidāya, “O my two masters”: the print has the nominative dual sayyidā- before the suffix; Classical, which puts a vocative of this kind in the accusative, would have yā sayyidayya. It is vocalised as printed. innahu yaʿizzu ʿalayya qatlukumā, “it is grievous to me, the killing of you two”: -hu is the pronoun of the matter, and ʿazza ʿalā, “to be hard on”, takes ʿalā for the one pained. qatlukumā, “your killing”: the verbal noun, with the dual suffix standing for the ones killed. The shaddas of جرّد, يعزّ and عليّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَهَلْ لَكُمَا مِنْ حَاجَةٍ فَأَقْضِيَهَا أَوْ وَصِيَّةٍ فَأُنْفِذَهَا أَوْ رِسَالَةٍ فَأُبَلِّغَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-hal lakumā min ḥājatin fa-aqḍiyahā aw waṣiyyatin fa-unfidhahā aw risālatin fa-uballighahā
sentences.l: So is-there for-you-two any need, so-that-I-fulfil-it, or a-charge, so-that-I-carry-it-out, or a-message, so-that-I-deliver-it?
sentences.i: Have you any wish that I may fulfil, any last charge that I may carry out, or any message that I may deliver?
sentences.n: hal lakumā min ḥājatin, “is there for you two any need?”: li- marks the ones who have it, and min after a question, before an indefinite noun, means “any”; waṣiyyatin and risālatin share its genitive. Each is answered by fa- with the subjunctive, fa-aqḍiyahā, fa-unfidhahā, fa-uballighahā, “so that I may …”: the fa- of a result after a question. waṣiyya, “a charge, a last will”. anfadha, Form IV, “to carry out (an order or a will)”; the letters would equally allow Form II, fa-unaffidhahā, with the same sense. ballagha, Form II, “to make reach, deliver”; the shadda of فابلّغها is printed. The three end alike in -hā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ مَالَنَا حَاجَةٌ وَأَمَّا مِنْ جِهَةِ الْوَصِيَّةِ فَإِنِّي أُوصِيكَ أَنْ تَجْعَلَ أَخِي الْأَسْعَدَ مِنْ تَحْتُ وَأَنَا مِنْ فَوْقُ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تَقَعَ عَلَيَّ الضَّرْبَةُ أَوَّلًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu mā lanā ḥājatun wa-ammā min jihati al-waṣiyyati fa-innī ūṣīka an tajʿala akhī al-Asʿada min taḥtu wa-anā min fawqu li-ajli an taqaʿa ʿalayya al-ḍarbatu awwalan
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad: Not to-us (is) a-need. And-as-for (from the) side (of) the-charge, then-indeed-I charge-you that you-put my-brother al-Asʿad from below and-I from above, for-the-sake-of that falls upon-me the-blow first.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said: We have no wish. As for a last charge, I charge you to put my brother al-Asʿad underneath and me on top, so that the blow falls on me first.
sentences.n: mā lanā ḥājatun, “we have no need”: the print runs mā lanā together as مالنا. wa-ammā … fa-, “and as for …”: ammā is always answered by fa-. min jihati, “on the side of, as regards”. ūṣīka an, “I charge you that”: Form IV awṣā, of the same root as waṣiyya. min taḥtu, min fawqu, “from below, from above”: the adverbs, cut off from a following noun, end in an invariable -u. wa-anā min fawqu, “and I on top”: rather than repeating the verb with an object, wa-tajʿalanī min fawqu, the Arabic adds a short nominal clause with the independent pronoun anā, “and I (am) on top”. li-ajli an, “for the sake of (it) that”, so that, with the subjunctive. The shadda of عليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ مِنْ قَتْلِنَا وَوَصَلْتَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَقَالَ لَكَ مَا سَمِعْتَ مِنْهُمَا قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِمَا فَقُلْ لَهُ إِنَّ وَلَدَيْكَ يَقْرَآنِكَ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā faraghta min qatlinā wa-waṣalta ilā al-maliki wa-qāla laka mā samiʿta minhumā qabla mawtihimā fa-qul lahu inna waladayka yaqraʾānika al-salāma
sentences.l: And-when you-have-finished from killing-us and-arrived to the-king, and-he-said to-you: What did-you-hear from-them-two before their-death?, then-say to-him: Indeed your-two-sons read-you the-greeting,
sentences.i: When you have done with killing us and come to the king, and he asks you, “What did you hear from them before they died?”, tell him: Your two sons send you their greeting,
sentences.n: fa-idhā with the perfect looks to the future: “when you have finished”. faragha min, “to be done with”: min marks the task. mā samiʿta minhumā: mā is here the question “what?”. The answer to idhā is introduced by fa-: fa-qul lahu, “then say to him”. yaqraʾānika al-salāma, “they read you the greeting”, the usual phrase for sending one's greetings: Classical says qaraʾa ʿalayhi al-salāma, or with Form IV aqraʾahu al-salāma, and the print has Form I with the person as a direct object, the everyday usage. The آ of يقرآنك is printed.

sentences.t: وَيَقُولَانِ لَكَ إِنَّكَ لَا تَعْلَمُ هَلْ هُمَا بَرِيآنِ أَوْ مُذْنِبَانِ وَقَدْ قَتَلْتَهُمَا وَمَا تَحَقَّقْتَ ذَنْبَهُمَا وَمَا نَظَرْتَ فِي حَالِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-yaqūlāni laka innaka lā taʿlamu hal humā barīʾāni aw mudhnibāni wa-qad qataltahumā wa-mā taḥaqqaqta dhanbahumā wa-mā naẓarta fī ḥālihimā
sentences.l: and-they-two-say to-you: Indeed-you do-not know whether they-two (are) two-innocent or two-guilty; and-(yet) you-have-killed-them-two, and-not did-you-make-sure-of their-guilt, and-not did-you-look into their-case.
sentences.i: and they say to you: You do not know whether they are innocent or guilty, and yet you have put them to death without making sure of their guilt or looking into their case.
sentences.n: The message is framed in the third person, “they say to you … whether they are innocent”, though the brothers are speaking of themselves. hal, “whether”, opens an indirect question. barīʾāni, “two innocent ones”, dual of barīʾ, which the print spells with a madda over the alif, بريآن, kept here; mudhnibāni, “two guilty ones”, dual of mudhnib, active participle of Form IV adhnaba, “to sin”. wa-qad qataltahumā, “when you have killed them”: a circumstantial clause, spoken as though the deed were already done. taḥaqqaqa, Form V, “to make sure of”, takes its object directly. naẓara fī, “to look into, examine”: fī marks the matter examined. The rhyme falls on dhanbahumā / ḥālihimā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَهُ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma anshadahu hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then he-recited-to-him these-two verses:
sentences.i: Then he recited these two verses to him:
sentences.n: anshadahu, “he recited to him”: anshada, Form IV, takes the hearer as one object and the verses as another. It is read here as narrative, al-Amjad reciting to the treasurer verses for him to pass on to the king; the letters equally allow the imperative anshidhu, “recite to him”, still inside al-Amjad's instructions (“then recite to him these two verses”), and “which you have heard” in the next sentence fits either reading.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ النِّسَاءَ شَيَاطِينٌ خُلِقْنَ لَنَا * اَعُوْذُ بِاللهِ مِنْ كَيْدِ الشَّيَاطِينِ
فَهُنَّ اَصْلُ الْبَلِيَّاتِ الَّتِي ظَهَرَتْ * بَيْنَ الْبَرِيَّةِ فِى الدُّنْيَا وَفِى الدِّينِ
sentences.tr:
inna al-nisāʾa shayāṭīnun khuliqna lanā * aʿūdhu bi-Allāhi min kaydi al-shayāṭīni
fa-hunna aṣlu al-baliyyāti allatī ẓaharat * bayna al-bariyyati fī al-dunyā wa-fī al-dīni
sentences.l:
Indeed the-women (are) devils created for-us; * I-take-refuge in-God from (the) scheming (of) the-devils.
So-they (are the) root (of) the-afflictions which have-appeared * among the-creation, in the-world and-in the-faith.
sentences.i:
Women are devils, created for our sake; * I take refuge in God from the cunning of devils.
They are the root of every affliction that has appeared * among mankind, in this world and in matters of faith.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -īni: al-shayāṭīni, al-dīni. shayāṭīnun, “devils”, is a broken plural that Classical declines without tanwīn; the print gives it tanwīn, which the poets allow themselves. khuliqna lanā, “they were created for us”: the passive of khalaqa with the feminine plural ending -na; li- marks the ones they are made for. aʿūdhu bi-Allāhi min, “I take refuge in God from”: ʿādha takes bi- for the protector and min for what one is shielded from; it echoes the Qurʾānic aʿūdhu bi-Allāhi mina al-shayṭāni al-rajīmi. al-dunyā wa-al-dīn, “this world and religion”: all things, worldly and spiritual. The print writes اِنَّ, اَعُوْذُ and اَصْلُ with a bare alif, puts a sukūn on the long vowel of اَعُوْذُ, and spells fī with ى, فِى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ مَا نُرِيدُ مِنْكَ إِلَّا أَنْ تُبَلِّغَهُ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ اللَّذَيْنِ سَمِعْتَهُمَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla al-Amjadu mā nurīdu minka illā an tuballighahu hādhayni al-baytayni alladhayni samiʿtahumā
sentences.l: Then said al-Amjad: Not we-want from-you except that you-deliver-to-him these-two verses which you-have-heard-them.
sentences.i: Then al-Amjad said: All we ask of you is that you carry to him these two verses you have heard.
sentences.n: The print has ما تريد منك, a misprint for ما نريد منك, corrected here: “you do not want from you” gives no sense, and al-Amjad speaks for them both. mā … illā an, “we want nothing but that”, so “all we want is that”. tuballighahu hādhayni al-baytayni, “that you make these two verses reach him”: Form II ballagha takes two objects, the person and the thing delivered. alladhayni samiʿtahumā, “the two which you heard them”: Arabic picks up the antecedent inside the relative clause with a pronoun, here the dual -humā. The shaddas of الّا and تبلّغه are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
